title: Kerala Launches 'Be a Malayali for a Day' Campaign to Reinvent Tourism Around Experiences
excerpt: The southern Indian state is shifting from scenic postcard marketing to immersive cultural tourism, with Onam festivities, backwater stays, and Ayurvedic retreats anchoring the new strategy.
body:
• Kerala launched "Be a Malayali for a Day," a new experiential tourism campaign that invites visitors to participate in local traditions rather than just observe them.
  • Tourism Minister P.A. Mohamed Riyas announced the initiative as part of a broader shift from "come see Kerala" to "come experience Kerala."
  • The state is pushing to grant industry status to tourism, with the process in its final stages, which would unlock tax benefits and easier financing for hospitality businesses.
  • Onam festivals, traditional boat races, Ayurvedic wellness programs, and backwater homestays will serve as flagship tourism products under the new strategy.

From Sightseeing to Living the Culture

Kerala's tourism department unveiled a new campaign called "Be a Malayali for a Day" that marks a deliberate pivot in how India's most tourism-dependent state markets itself to the world. Rather than promoting beaches, hill stations, and houseboats as things to look at, the campaign positions Kerala as a place to live like a local — cooking an Onasadya feast, rowing through backwaters with fishermen, or learning Kathakali from village performers.

Tourism Minister P.A. Mohamed Riyas framed it as an evolution. "The shift is from 'come see Kerala' to 'come experience Kerala,'" he said while announcing the campaign, which will be rolled out across international markets with a focus on cultural diversity, traditional art forms, and festival tourism.

"The shift is from 'come see Kerala' to 'come experience Kerala.'"

— P.A. Mohamed Riyas, Tourism Minister, Kerala

Onam as a Tourism Product

Central to the new approach is packaging Kerala's festivals — particularly Onam — as structured tourism experiences. The state plans to offer visitors curated access to Onasadya banquets, the elaborate vegetarian feast served on banana leaves, as well as front-row participation in Vallamkali boat races, Pulikali tiger dances, Kummattikali masked performances, and Karadikali harvest celebrations.

The valla sadya, a communal riverside feast tied to boat race festivals, is being positioned as a signature culinary tourism draw. The idea is to move beyond the standard Kerala backwater cruise and embed visitors in the rituals that define the state's cultural calendar.

Industry Status and Infrastructure

Kerala is also working to formalize tourism's economic standing. The process of granting industry status to the tourism sector is in its final stages, according to Riyas. The classification would give hotels, resorts, and tourism operators access to industrial tax incentives, subsidized land allotments, and priority lending — measures that could accelerate private investment in a sector that accounts for roughly 10% of the state's GDP.

Alongside the industry status push, cultural events and festivals will be formally included in the state's official tourism calendar. That move would ensure consistent government funding and marketing support for events that have historically relied on local or temple-level organization.

Medical and Ayurvedic Tourism

The campaign also highlights Kerala's established position in medical and Ayurvedic tourism. The state already attracts hundreds of thousands of wellness tourists annually, and the new strategy aims to integrate Ayurvedic retreats more tightly with cultural experiences — pairing a Panchakarma detox with a temple festival visit, for instance, rather than treating them as separate itineraries.

Backwater tourism, which has been Kerala's marquee product for decades, is being repositioned with an emphasis on homestay experiences and community-run tourism cooperatives rather than commercial houseboat fleets.

A Draw for the Diaspora

For the large NRI Malayali community — estimated at over 2 million in the Gulf states alone, with sizable populations in the US, UK, and Canada — the campaign carries a different appeal. Second-generation diaspora members who grew up hearing about Onam and Vishu but have never experienced them firsthand are a natural audience for the "Be a Malayali for a Day" pitch.

The experiential format also addresses a recurring gap in diaspora travel: visiting family in Kerala without meaningfully engaging with the state's cultural infrastructure. The campaign's curated experiences could turn routine family visits into structured cultural reconnections.

What's Next

Kerala plans to roll out the campaign across key international markets ahead of the October-March peak tourism season. The Onam festival period in September will serve as the first major test of the experiential tourism model, with the state tourism department coordinating with local communities and cultural organizations to deliver the promised immersive experiences.
